title: Rental technology can widen housing access while shifting screening, pricing, and surveillance power
source_unit: U.S. Government Accountability Office GAO-25-107196 review of rental advertising platforms, tenant-screening tools, rent-setting software, and facial-recognition technology
geography: United States private and subsidized rental housing; selected companies, public housing agencies, federal agencies, industry groups, and advocacy organizations

observations.period: 2019–2025 GAO review; selected rental property-technology tools

product_types.value: advertising platforms, tenant-screening tools, rent-setting software, and facial-recognition technology

functions.value: advertising, touring, leasing, financial management, screening, rent setting, and building access

benefit_route.value: tools can make it easier to search, view, lease, manage, and secure rental housing

observations.method: GAO review of federal, academic, industry, and advocacy reports; agency guidance, legal cases, and enforcement; and interviews with four federal agencies, 12 companies, 10 public housing agencies, industry associations, and advocacy organizations.
observations.uncertainty: The company, agency, and stakeholder samples were purposively selected and are not generalizable to all rental tools, landlords, public housing agencies, or renters.
observations.subgroup: Private and subsidized rental housing, with selected advertising, screening, pricing, and access technologies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital tools can reduce search and management costs or improve building safety; their presence does not establish a renter's loss of access or control.

observations.period: 2019–2025; rental screening, pricing, advertising, and privacy risks

denominator.unit: selected rental proptech types assessed for benefits and risks

screening_accuracy_risk.value: inaccurate or outdated criminal, eviction, credit, or other records can lead to unwarranted denials and housing instability

pricing_power_risk.value: rent-setting algorithms may reduce bargaining power and may be associated with higher rents or lower occupancy during some market conditions

surveillance_risk.value: facial recognition may misidentify demographic groups or allow surveillance information to be used without renter consent

advertising_risk.value: algorithmic targeting or listing language may steer or discourage protected groups before they can apply

observations.method: GAO synthesis of reviewed studies and interviews; reported pricing associations and potential risks are kept separate from national prevalence or causal estimates.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not estimate how often inaccurate screening, algorithmic price effects, surveillance misuse, or discriminatory steering occurs across the rental market.
observations.subgroup: Renters and applicants, especially people affected by criminal, eviction, disability, familial-status, race, sex, or other protected-status classifications.
observations.counterinterpretation: Screening can help owners verify information, facial recognition can improve security, and algorithms may improve matching or reduce fraud; risk mechanisms are not proof of unlawful treatment in every case.

observations.period: As of May 2026; federal oversight and public-housing guidance

denominator.unit: public housing agencies interviewed by GAO about facial-recognition technology

additional_direction_requested.unit: public housing agencies saying they would benefit from additional facial-recognition guidance

hud_guidance.value: HUD guidance was high-level and did not provide specific direction on privacy risks, law-enforcement data sharing, permitted uses, consent, data management, or accuracy

correction_status.value: HUD reported that technical assistance was being developed and estimated written guidance would be completed in December 2026

enforcement_visibility.value: federal agencies pursued actions on alleged discriminatory advertising and inaccurate screening data, including settlements and enforcement

observations.method: GAO comparison of federal oversight, public-housing-agency interviews, agency guidance, settlements, and enforcement actions.
observations.uncertainty: The ten-agency interview result is not a national public-housing census; planned guidance is not completed implementation, and enforcement actions do not measure all affected renters.
observations.subgroup: Public housing agencies and renters subject to facial-recognition access or other rental proptech controls.
observations.counterinterpretation: Agency enforcement and forthcoming guidance can provide meaningful correction even while standardized operational rules remain incomplete.

related_sources.claim: Official full GAO report provides tool descriptions, risk mechanisms, oversight actions, and methodological boundaries.
Related GAO homebuying proptech review supplies a separate buyer and mortgage-market comparison; this record does not pool its findings.

boundary: This record identifies a rental-housing digital interface where search, screening, pricing, advertising, surveillance, privacy, and fair-housing oversight meet. It does not establish a national discrimination, rent-increase, privacy-loss, denial, eviction, housing-instability, trust, or political-action rate.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official GAO product page used for extracted product, risk, oversight, and recommendation findings; full report is linked but not retained in this record.
